analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable standards for immigrant detention and phases out private, for-profit detention facilities.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2023 by Senator Booker with 6 cosponsors, the bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Homeland Security to set enforceable standards for the facilities where it detains immigrants, with annual unannounced inspections by its Inspector General, fines and contract termination for facilities that fail, and public reporting of any death in custody. It would ban detaining children and solitary confinement, replace automatic detention of asylum seekers with individualized custody hearings and a presumption of release, and require the government—rather than private companies and county jails—to own and operate all detention facilities within three years. It would also replace ankle-monitor programs with community-based case management run by nonprofits.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants and asylum seekers held in federal immigration custody, plus their families: they would gain enforceable health and safety standards, faster public reporting of deaths, an end to solitary confinement and child detention, bond amounts tied to ability to pay, a presumption of release at a hearing within 72 hours, and legal recourse in court if injured by a standards violation [S2][S3]. Taxpayers would also gain transparency, since inspection reports and detention contracts would become public records [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Facilities would have to meet the American Bar Association's civil immigration detention standards, checked by at least annual unannounced Inspector General inspections, with fines of at least 10 percent of a facility's contract value for a first failure and contract termination after repeated failures [S2][S3].

Any death in custody would have to be reported to Congress within 24 hours and investigated within 30 days with a root-cause analysis and a public report; inspection reports and detention contracts would become public records, and a monthly public database would track every facility's population and conditions [S2][S3].

The bill bans detaining anyone under 18 in ICE custody, bans solitary confinement, and repeals mandatory detention for asylum seekers, replacing it with a custody hearing within 72 hours, a presumption of release, the least restrictive conditions, and bonds set based on ability to pay [S2][S3].

Within three years, DHS could no longer contract with any private, for-profit company or jail to hold immigrants or run alternatives-to-detention programs; facilities would have to be owned and operated by DHS or nonprofits, and ankle-monitor surveillance would be replaced with community-based case management offering housing, medical care, and legal services [S3].
Detainees injured by a violation of the standards could sue in federal court for compensatory damages and attorney fees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private prison companies and the county jails that profit from ICE detention contracts would lose that revenue, and electronic-monitoring providers would lose the ankle-monitor business. DHS and taxpayers would bear the cost of buying, building, or operating detention capacity in-house and of funding the new community-based case management program. Enforcement and court systems would absorb added custody hearings and litigation [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison companies and ICE detention contractors

drawbacks.text: Requiring DHS to own and operate every detention facility within three years would be expensive and logistically difficult, since the government does not currently control enough beds, and the bill gives no funding mechanism for the transition [S3].

Creating a presumption of release and barring reliance on a criminal conviction or arrest as the sole basis for detention would make it harder to hold people accused of crimes in immigration custody, a trade-off critics of bail-style reforms point to as a public-safety risk [S3].

Banning ankle monitors outright, even as one option among alternatives, removes a tool ICE currently uses to track people released into the community, and the community-based case management program it substitutes would be new and untested at scale [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core—binding standards, independent inspections, public reporting of deaths, and an end to child detention and solitary confinement—addresses documented problems in immigration detention at modest cost. The largest costs fall on a concentrated industry rather than the general public. The riskiest design choices are the three-year, unfunded mandate that DHS own all facilities and the blanket ban on electronic monitoring, which could create capacity and tracking problems during the transition. On balance the benefits to detained people and to transparency outweigh the costs, though the phase-out would need funding and planning to work.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2023 and never came up for a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the Dignity for Detained Immigrants Act of 2023 in the Senate on April 19, 2023 [S1][S5].
Six senators cosponsored it—five Democrats and one independent—according to the bill's cosponsor list [S4].

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and the action history shows no further action—no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House companion action—before the 118th Congress ended [S5].

The bill's provisions included enforceable detention standards, unannounced inspections, a phase-out of for-profit and jail-based detention within three years, a ban on detaining children and on solitary confinement, and repeal of mandatory detention for asylum seekers [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit detention companies and the jails holding ICE contracts kept their revenue streams, since the three-year phase-out never took effect, and detention conditions remained governed by the weaker pre-existing regime. Detained immigrants gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought the six original cosponsors onto it.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: The committee his panel received the bill in never held a markup or advanced it; no committee vote occurred in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; all seven supporters were Democrats or the independent Senator Sanders, with no Republican cosponsor recorded, and the bill stalled in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Private, for-profit detention contractors (e.g., GEO Group, CoreCivic)
industries.note: These companies hold most ICE detention bed contracts, funded by federal appropriations; the bill would terminate their contracts within three years and require DHS to own and run facilities itself. Their business model depends on holding people in custody, so their interest runs against detainees seeking release and better conditions.

industries.industry: County and local jails holding ICE detainees
industries.note: The bill bars contracts with any public or private for-profit entity operating a detention facility, which would end counties' ICE jail revenue alongside the private contractors'. Jails profit per bed-night occupied, an incentive that runs against detainees' interest in release and humane conditions.

The bill bans ankle monitors and other electronic surveillance as alternatives to detention and forbids charging detainees fees for monitoring programs, replacing a per-person surveillance revenue stream with government-funded community case management.

The bill directs DHS to contract with experienced nonprofits for case management—housing, medical, legal, and social services—for people released from custody, creating a new federal funding channel for organizations already serving immigrant communities.
